name: Rhizodus
fact: Possibly the largest freshwater fish of the Devonian with teeth the size of bananas. A lobe-finned predator related to the ancestors of land vertebrates, Rhizodus lurked in river channels and could ambush prey from the shallows like a modern crocodile.

name: Meganeura
fact: The biggest insect that EVER lived — a dragonfly with a wingspan like a seagull! It was a fierce predator of smaller insects and possibly small amphibians. High oxygen is what let insects grow this enormous.

name: Arthropleura
fact: A millipede as big as a car! Totally harmless — it just ate rotting plants and fungi. It was the biggest land invertebrate in all of history. Imagine encountering this on a forest path!
know: The largest arthropod that ever lived — a millipede relative up to 2.6 m long. For over 150 years no head had been found; in 2024, CT scans of juveniles from France finally showed one, with stalked eyes.

name: Hylonomus
fact: One of the FIRST true reptiles! Unlike amphibians, it could lay eggs on dry land without returning to water. A tiny lizard-like animal that started a lineage leading to every reptile, dinosaur, and mammal that ever lived.

name: Eryops
fact: A giant amphibian built like a flat, stocky crocodile. It was the top predator in many swampy environments. But it still had to lay eggs in water — the key weakness that reptiles would soon overcome forever.

name: Pulmonate Snail
fact: The first land snails with lungs instead of gills! They could breathe air and hydrate themselves in water. Still around today, they show how a sea creature can invade land and stick around for 360 million years.

name: Lepidodendron
fact: A scale tree - not a true tree but a giant club moss taller than a 10-story building. When these giants fell into swampy soil they did not fully rot because fungi had not yet evolved to digest lignin, slowly becoming the coal seams we burn today. Every piece of coal is fossilized Carboniferous forest.

name: Westlothiana
fact: Nicknamed Lizzie, Westlothiana is one of the earliest known amniotes - animals that lay eggs on land without needing water. This tiny reptile-like creature represents the point where vertebrate life finally broke its dependence on water for reproduction.

name: Edops
fact: A massive temnospondyl amphibian with a broad flat skull and powerful jaws. Like a modern giant salamander scaled up to the size of an alligator, Edops lurked at the water's edge and ambushed fish, smaller amphibians, and early reptiles.

name: Petrolacosaurus
fact: The earliest known diapsid reptile - the ancestor of all lizards, snakes, crocodiles, dinosaurs, and birds. Slender and lizard-like, Petrolacosaurus was a fast insect-hunter. Its skull design was so successful that 80% of living reptiles still use it.

name: Sigillaria
fact: A giant club moss cousin of Lepidodendron with vertical rows of hexagonal leaf scars on its trunk. Sigillaria had a single crown of long grass-like leaves at the top. Its fossils are found on every continent, proving the Carboniferous coal swamps were truly global.

name: Pulmonoscorpius
fact: A scorpion the length of a cat, from the oxygen-rich air of the Carboniferous. It breathed through book lungs, like scorpions today.

name: Tullimonstrum (Tully monster)
fact: Illinois's state fossil: eyes on a stiff crossbar and a long trunk ending in a toothed claw. Found by amateur collector Francis Tully in 1958.
debate: Nobody agrees what it was. A fish? A worm? A mollusc? Studies in 2016 and 2023 reached opposite conclusions.

name: Pederpes
fact: The first four-legged animal with feet that pointed forward for walking. It fills part of “Romer's gap”, a stretch of time once almost empty of land-animal fossils.

name: Crassigyrinus
fact: An eel-like water predator with tiny legs and huge jaws full of fangs — four legs did not mean leaving the water.

name: Falcatus
fact: A small shark relative. The males carried a long spine sweeping forward over the head — probably for display or courtship.

name: Archaeothyris
fact: One of the oldest known synapsids — the branch of the family tree that leads to mammals. It looked like a lizard but was on your side of the split.

name: Calamites
fact: A horsetail the size of a tree. Its relatives today grow knee-high in ditches.

name: Megarachne
fact: Described in 1980 as the largest spider ever. A second fossil found in 2005 showed it was a sea scorpion with a broad head — the giant spider never existed.

name: Akmonistion
fact: An “anvil shark”: in males, the fin on its back was a flat-topped brush covered in teeth-like scales, like a hairbrush on its back.

name: Edestus
fact: A shark relative with curved blades of teeth in both jaws that met like the blades of scissors.

name: Bandringa
fact: A shark with a long snout like a paddlefish. Young ones lived in swampy nurseries close to shore, then moved out to sea as adults (2014).

name: Mazothairos
fact: A giant insect with six wings — a small extra pair behind its head — and a beak for sucking plant juices.

name: Euphoberia
fact: A millipede covered in long forked spines, probably to put off predators.

name: Dendrerpeton
fact: An amphibian found, with early reptiles, inside the hollow stumps of fossil trees at Joggins — trapped where the trunks had rotted out.

name: Ophiderpeton
fact: A legless, snake-like amphibian — over 200 vertebrae and no limbs at all. Real snakes would not appear for another 150 million years.

name: Proterogyrinus
fact: A heavy-headed water predator with stout legs, related to the ancestors of reptiles.

name: Spinoaequalis
fact: A small reptile with a flattened, paddle-like tail — the first reptile known to have gone back to the water. Reptiles kept doing this for 300 million years.

name: Medullosa
fact: It looks like a fern but made seeds — some the size of hen's eggs. Seed ferns were among the first plants to make seeds.
